claims.claim: Deployment pipelines have 2 to 10 stages, default three.

Data isn't copied between stages, semantic model refresh required; existing items overwritten with ID, URL and permissions unchanged; autobinding to linked items in the target stage; REST APIs available.
Rule types: data source, parameter, default lakehouse; defined in the target stage; apply from the next deployment.
CI/CD options include Git-based release options and deployment pipelines; many organisations use a hybrid.

concept_html:
Git integration (lesson C10-L1) versions your items. Deployment pipelines move them between environments. A pipeline has 2 to 10 stages, with Development, Test and Production as the default three. Each stage is a workspace (Microsoft Learn, checked September 2026).

What a deployment copies. When you deploy from one stage to the next, Fabric copies item content and metadata to the target stage. It does not copy data. After deploying a semantic model, you refresh it in the target stage. After deploying a lakehouse, you load its tables there.

Overwrite, not replace. If the item already exists in the target stage, Fabric overwrites its content. The item's ID, URL and permissions stay the same, so reports and links in production keep working.

Deployment rules give each stage its own settings:

  • Data source rules: point a semantic model at the production database, not the test one.
  • Parameter rules: set a parameter's value per stage.
  • Default lakehouse rules: attach a notebook to the stage's own lakehouse.

You define a rule in the target stage, on the item. It applies from the next deployment into that stage.

Autobinding. If a deployed item depends on another item, such as a report on a semantic model, and the linked item exists in the target stage, Fabric binds to the target copy automatically.

Compare shows which items differ between two stages before you deploy. Use it every time. The deployment pipelines REST APIs automate the same steps from a build system.

Many teams combine the tools. Developers work in Git-connected workspaces and merge through pull requests. The merged branch updates the Development stage, and deployment pipelines promote tested content to Test and Production. Microsoft's CI/CD guidance also describes Git-only release options, so pick one and document it.

exercises.prompt: Model deployment rules. Write `deployed_settings(source: dict[str, str], rules: dict[str, dict[str, str]], stage: str) -> dict[str, str]`. `source` holds an item's settings in the source stage. `rules` maps a stage name to the settings its rules override. Return the settings in `stage`: the source values, with that stage's rules applied. Do not modify `source`. Raise `ValueError` if a rule names a setting the item does not have.
exercises.prompt_html: Model deployment rules. Write deployed_settings(source: dict[str, str], rules: dict[str, dict[str, str]], stage: str) -> dict[str, str]. source holds an item's settings in the source stage. rules maps a stage name to the settings its rules override. Return the settings in stage: the source values, with that stage's rules applied. Do not modify source. Raise ValueError if a rule names a setting the item does not have.
exercises.solution:
def deployed_settings(
    source: dict[str, str], rules: dict[str, dict[str, str]], stage: str
) -> dict[str, str]:
    """Item settings in a target stage after its deployment rules apply.

    Args:
        source: Settings in the source stage.
        rules: Stage name to the settings its rules override.
        stage: Target stage.

    Returns:
        A new dict of settings for the target stage.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If a rule names a setting the item does not have.
    """
    stage_rules = rules.get(stage, {})
    unknown = set(stage_rules) - set(source)
    if unknown:
        raise ValueError(f"rules for unknown settings: {sorted(unknown)}")
    return {**source, **stage_rules}

title: Deployment pipelines, dev to test to production
why_html: A team deployed a notebook from Test to Production. It still pointed at the test lakehouse, so for a week the production job wrote its gold tables into Test. The dashboard in Production read stale tables and nobody noticed. A default lakehouse rule on the notebook in the Production stage would have attached it to the production lakehouse on every deployment.
